text: A man in middle age is filmed at home over three years by his own cousin, which leaves the camera no visitor's distance to fall back on. Philly is intellectually disabled, and Ira Wohl's method is to stay: 111 minutes assembled out of ordinary hours that most documentaries would visit for an afternoon and then summarize. Three years is also long enough for a routine to change, which is the reason to shoot that long. What a family owes one of its own is never posed here as a question; it is simply what is happening at the table, on the sidewalk, in the room where the difficult talking gets done. The Academy gave it the documentary Oscar, and in Toronto the audience handed over the prize they vote on themselves. The camera keeps to tasks rather than events, and duration does the rest.

A warship is a closed town with a mast in the middle: whatever the story will need - water, timber, powder, a surgeon, an argument - has to be aboard before it sails. Peter Weir takes that literally and stays out there, 138 minutes of pursuit across two oceans after a French ship opens the film by damaging the British one badly. The chase belongs to the captain, and it is not free: every league gained is charged to a crew whose devotion outruns the odds. His closest friend aboard is the ship's surgeon, which puts the argument between glory and prudence inside a friendship instead of between ranks. The Academy's cinematography award went to this, and it shows less in the battles than in the weather and the work - rope, salt, low light, men keeping a wooden machine running.

The children are not in danger; they are overlooked, which is a slower kind of trouble and takes 139 minutes to work through. Turn-of-the-century London, a household where the father is elsewhere even when he is home, and a nanny who arrives with a method of her own: music, adventure, and time spent. The magic is the delivery system. The thing under repair is a man's attention, and Robert Stevenson's 1964 film is patient enough to let that take the full running time. The Academy gave its Best Actress prize to the nanny, and the National Film Registry keeps the picture on the national record. Two and a half hours is a serious sit for something aimed at children, and the length is where the family, rather than the enchantment, gets its due.

A sports film whose outcome is already public property has to find its suspense somewhere other than the scoreboard. This one looks on the practice court, in the years before anyone was watching, and hands its 144 minutes to the father rather than to the players - which is the real risk in the design, since Venus and Serena arrive with the whole future attached and Richard Williams has only a plan and the will to keep enforcing it. The Academy's Best Actor award went to him, and the National Board of Review placed the film in its top ten. What is actually at stake is not the careers, whose shape everyone already knows, but the household paying for them years in advance, on a schedule set by one certain man. Reinaldo Marcus Green shot it in 2021, long after both daughters had made his argument for him.

A sharecropping plantation in northern Florida, blindness at seven, and a mother who refused to make anything easier. That is the starting material; 152 minutes is how long the film takes to get from it to a sound nobody had assembled before. Ray Charles learned the Southern circuit room by room, then set gospel beside country - two traditions kept apart for reasons that had little to do with music. The mother's instruction, that he make his own way, is what the picture keeps testing, since a blind performer in that business had every reason to be handled rather than to decide. Taylor Hackford directed it in 2004; the Academy's Best Actor award and a National Board of Review top-ten place followed. The life is organized around the instrument, and the argument gets settled, each time, at the keyboard.

The tutorial is in deception - how to read a room, what to hide, when to let a stranger believe he is ahead. Fast Eddie Felson has been out of the game for years when he takes on Vincent Lauria, who has the talent and none of the patience: a kid who cannot bear to be underestimated, apprenticed to a man whose entire living came from being underestimated. That mismatch is the film, more than any single match is. Martin Scorsese shot it in 1986, 119 minutes of pool halls and road, with a partnership that works commercially and not at all otherwise. The Academy's Best Actor award went to Eddie, and the National Board of Review listed the film among its ten best that year. Two temperaments, one trade, and no agreement whatever about what winning is for.

Two Americans go over the wire and are shot, and by morning the barracks has decided that somebody inside sold them. Billy Wilder set a comedy in a German prison camp in 1953, eight years after the war, and the comedy is not at the expense of the dead - it is about a group that wants a suspect more than it wants evidence. J.J. Sefton runs the barracks black market, which makes him the readiest shape for suspicion to take: a man doing well where everyone else does without. That is the dare in the design, 120 minutes locked in one hut with a character nobody present wishes to defend and nowhere for him to go. The Academy's Best Actor award went to the part. Wilder gets his laughs and never softens the ground the men are standing on.

Three men are charged; the room that watched and cheered is not. That gap is the film's case, and it is a stranger legal proposition than the crime it follows from. Sarah Tobias is raped in a bar in front of an audience, the district attorney who takes the case settles it at a discount, and the survivor ends up the least consulted party in her own matter. What remains is everyone else who was in the bar. Pursuing them means Sarah gives the account again in open court, at length, to strangers with an interest in doubting her - a price the film puts on screen rather than around it. Jonathan Kaplan directed in 1988; the Academy's Best Actress award went to Sarah, and the National Board of Review named the film one of the year's ten best.

Everything that frightens the new wife arrives as a household detail: an object moved, footsteps on a floor above, a sound with no source. The house is doing the work, and it is a large one - a family mansion, staffed, holding no independent witness who is not either employed or a stranger. George Cukor kept the 1944 film almost entirely indoors for 114 minutes, and the confinement is the point: reduce a world to rooms and the people paid to keep them, and a woman's testimony about her own senses has nowhere to go for confirmation. The Academy gave it Best Actress and the award for black-and-white art direction, which is the right pairing. It sits on the National Film Registry. The performance and the furniture are running the same scheme.

A woman with no capital and one saleable skill opens a restaurant, and the film treats that as suspense, which it is. Mildred Pierce leaves a marriage and builds the business for a daughter with expensive tastes and nothing to give back, so the labor has a beneficiary who does not work. The genre label says crime; most of the running time is work. Michael Curtiz shot it in 1945, 111 minutes in black and white, with the threat coming from inside the household rather than from anywhere outside it. What stands to be lost is not affection, which is never in doubt, but solvency and standing - the two things she made herself, and the only two her daughter knows how to spend. The Academy's Best Actress award went to Mildred, and the National Film Registry keeps the picture.

In 1968 a studio committed 155 minutes to a single performer, a picture built to be carried rather than shared. Fanny Brice came up in Jewish New York and reached the top of the business inside the Ziegfeld Follies, and the film gives most of its running time to the act itself, which is the honest way to shoot a comedienne. There is a built-in difficulty in that: the funny has to still be funny, decades later, in a different room. Running the other way is Nick Arnstein - charming, a gambler, her husband - so the marriage becomes a series of positions taken on incomplete information while the career only ever pays for work. The Academy's Best Actress award went to Brice, and the National Film Registry holds the picture. William Wyler directed, at a length that assumes an audience willing to sit and be performed at.

The verdict is already in when the film starts, which changes what a legal story can be about. Sunny von Bülow lies brain-dead; her husband Claus has been convicted of putting her there; he says he did not, and hires Alan Dershowitz to run the appeal. An appeal asks a narrower question than a trial - not what happened in the house, but whether the case that convicted him holds up - and Barbet Schroeder spends 111 minutes inside that distinction. The discomfort is structural. The work is technical, the client is rich and difficult to warm to, and the machinery is indifferent to both. The Academy's Best Actor award went to Claus, which is where the film keeps its uncertainty: a man asserting his innocence in a register no one can read, inside a process that has stopped caring how he sounds.

A romance between a hearing teacher and a deaf woman who cleans the school where he works has a problem of language before it has one of feeling. James Leeds arrives in New England for a post that assumes speech is the destination. Sarah Norman is already in the building, mopping its floors, withdrawn and in no hurry to be reached. Every exchange between them has to function twice - once between the two of them, once for an audience that may not sign - and 119 minutes of that is a formal difficulty most love stories never take on. The difference in station stays in the room: he holds the post with authority, she holds the one without, and the same institution pays both. Randa Haines directed in 1986; the Academy's Best Actress award went to Sarah. What is at risk is not the romance but the terms of it.

A man without money is attentive to a woman who will inherit a great deal, and nothing either of them says can settle what that means. New York in the 1840s: a doctor's house, a daughter whose days have contained no events worth the name, a suitor who is charming and poor. The trap is that sincerity cannot be proved here - every kindness is also evidence, every doubt is also a cruelty, and the man holding the money is the one appointed to judge. William Wyler keeps almost all of it in the parlors, 115 minutes of talk in which the decisive moves concern the disposition of property and are made in the language of feeling. The Academy gave the picture its Best Actress award and its prize for black-and-white art direction, and the National Film Registry keeps it on the national record.
